title: Festivals differ
hook: Vesak, Hanamatsuri, Saga Dawa: one birth, many calendars

segments.voice: Yesterday, robes and colors: saffron, maroon, gray and black, and the rice fields of Magadha sewn into each. Your line was the robe's color. What color caught your eye? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-six.

A small shrine sits on a temple step, its roof covered in fresh flowers. Inside stands a statue of a baby, no taller than a teacup, one hand pointing up to the sky and one pointing down to the earth. A line of children waits with a bamboo ladle. One by one, each dips the ladle in a bowl of sweet tea and pours it gently over the baby's head. Then they giggle and drink a little themselves. This is a birthday party. The guest of honor was born a very long time ago. Today: festivals differ.
screen: `A SHRINE COVERED IN FLOWERS.` → `A BABY POINTING UP AND DOWN.` → `SWEET TEA ON HIS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Why pour water on a baby statue? The answer is in a Pali discourse, the Discourse on Wonderful and Marvelous Qualities. It tells of the Buddha's birth: the newborn stands, takes seven steps, looks out over the quarters and speaks. And two streams of water appear from the sky, one cool and one warm, to bathe him and his mother. The children with the ladle are retelling that moment with their hands. So the birth is shared. The days are not. First, Vesak, kept by Theravada communities in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia on a full moon in the month of Vesakha. Theravada tradition marks three things on that one day: the birth, the awakening and the passing away. Lanterns, white clothes, temple visits, food given freely. Second, Hanamatsuri, the flower festival, the scene you just heard. In Japan, it honors the birth alone, with the flowered shrine recalling the garden at Lumbini where tradition says he was born. Korea, China and Vietnam keep their own birthday celebrations by their own calendars, with lanterns and the same bathing of the baby. Third, Saga Dawa, a whole month of practice for Tibetan communities. Its full-moon day honors the awakening and the passing, and in some reckonings the birth as well. People walk circuits around holy places, give to those in need, and some avoid eating meat for the month. So in one year, the same birth may be celebrated on several different days, by communities that each have good reasons for their count. Nobody here is late to the party. They just keep different calendars.
screen: `TWO STREAMS OF WATER.` · `VESAK: THREE MOMENTS, ONE DAY.` · `HANAMATSURI: THE FLOWER FESTIVAL.` · `SAGA DAWA: A WHOLE MONTH.` · then, large: `ONE BIRTH, MANY DAYS.`

segments.voice: If you'd like to try it, sit and let the breath settle. Call up the little shrine of flowers and the children with the ladle. On each out-breath, picture a little water poured, one cool stream, one warm. Let it wash over a birth you're grateful for: your own, a child's, a friend's, anyone's. When the bell rings, if you're curious, look up when Vesak and Hanamatsuri fall this year, and notice how far apart two calendars can put the same birthday. The bell holds the time.
Festivals differ. Vesak, Hanamatsuri, Saga Dawa: different days, different customs, all honoring the same life. Today's word.
Your line: one birth, many days. Today, when someone marks something on a different day than you would, let both days count. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists keep Vesak with temple visits, lanterns and giving; in Japan, Hanamatsuri is kept by pouring sweet tea over a baby Buddha statue in a flower-covered shrine; Tibetan Buddhists keep Saga Dawa as a month of practice, giving and circling holy places.

fork.setup: you're in Japan at a flower-covered shrine with a small baby Buddha inside. a bowl of sweet tea and a ladle sit beside it. what do people do?
options: leave the tea as an offering, untouched.
pour the tea gently over the baby's head.
drink the tea and walk away.
fork.reveal: they bathe the statue with sweet tea, recalling the cool and warm streams that, in the text, bathed the newborn.

original.note: Pali Vesakha: the month whose full moon Theravada communities keep as Vesak.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhists have one birthday for the Buddha.
what it means: Vesak, Hanamatsuri and Saga Dawa honor the same life on different days, with different customs.
what a scholar hears: the birth wonders of a Pali discourse, seven steps and two streams of water, behind the bathing of the baby Buddha.

sources.ref: Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 123), the birth wonders

notes: MN 123 paraphrased: the newborn stands, takes seven steps, surveys the quarters and speaks; two streams of water from the sky, cool and warm, bathe him and his mother. Confirm the count of steps and the waters.
Vesak on the full moon of Vesakha marking birth, awakening and passing, per Theravada tradition; confirm.
Hanamatsuri honoring the birth only, sweet tea (amacha) poured over the statue, flowered shrine recalling Lumbini; confirm.
Saga Dawa: the full-moon day (Saga Dawa Duchen) honors awakening and passing, and in some reckonings the birth; circumambulation, giving, some avoid meat for the month. Confirm the birth wording.
Korea, China and Vietnam birthday celebrations named without dates; confirm.
Original: वेसाख; confirm spelling and that Vesak is named for this month.
Editor: 'in one spring' changed to 'in one year' (Saga Dawa can fall in early summer); cut the unsourced calendar claim 'lunar months and solar ones rarely line up'.
